title: Apple Patches Hide My Email Flaw That Exposed Real User Addresses
excerpt: Apple fixed a vulnerability in its iCloud+ Hide My Email feature that allowed senders to uncover users' real email addresses through spam-rejected messages, more than a year after it was first reported.
body:
• Apple deployed a patch on July 3 for a Hide My Email vulnerability that leaked real email addresses when messages were rejected as spam, but independent testing reproduced the flaw as late as July 17.
  • EasyOptOuts co-founder Tyler Murphy first reported the bug to Apple in June 2025; Apple only addressed it after 404 Media publicized the issue in early July 2026.
  • A class action lawsuit has been filed against Apple, alleging the company violated California consumer protection laws by advertising Hide My Email as a privacy feature while knowing it was compromised.
  • Security researchers warn that email addresses linked to Hide My Email aliases created before July 7, 2026 should be treated as potentially exposed.

Apple has patched a vulnerability in its Hide My Email feature that allowed senders to discover the real email addresses of iCloud+ subscribers, the company confirmed to 404 Media on Monday. The fix, which Apple says was deployed on July 3, comes more than 13 months after the flaw was first reported — and only after sustained media pressure forced the company's hand.

A Year of Broken Promises

Hide My Email is a paid feature bundled with Apple's iCloud+ subscription. It generates random email aliases — typically two random words followed by a number at the icloud.com domain — that forward messages to a user's real inbox. The feature is designed to prevent websites, services, and third parties from linking a user's activity across platforms.

https://x.com/MacRumors/status/2079615135774290266

Tyler Murphy, co-founder of privacy firm EasyOptOuts, discovered the vulnerability and reported it to Apple in June 2025. Over the following year, Apple repeatedly claimed the issue was under investigation or had been resolved. Murphy found the flaw remained exploitable after each claimed fix, including one Apple said it deployed in March 2026.

"In our limited tests with volunteers, 100% of Hide My Email addresses were exploitable."

— Tyler Murphy, co-founder, EasyOptOuts

"Over the following year, Apple repeatedly claimed the issue was under investigation or had been resolved."

"Over the following year, Apple repeatedly claimed the issue was under investigation or had been resolved."

"Over the following year, Apple repeatedly claimed the issue was under investigation or had been resolved."

Frustrated by Apple's inaction, Murphy contacted 404 Media, which published a report on July 1 without disclosing exploitation details. Apple told the outlet it deployed a patch on July 3 that fully resolved the issue.

How the Exploit Worked

With Apple's confirmation that the bug is fixed, 404 Media and EasyOptOuts have disclosed the mechanism. Sending a targeted Hide My Email user a message that was rejected as spam caused the recipient's actual email address to appear in email server logs. The process required no sophisticated hacking — for many major email providers, the leak was triggered automatically when an email bounced, even if the original message was legitimate.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=R98FmAUOT0U

Murphy and EasyOptOuts co-founder Ben Weiner cautioned that the fix does not eliminate all risk. Mail transfer logs from before the patch may still contain exposed addresses.

"We'd assume that any hidden email address linked to a Hide My Email address created before July 7, 2026, may have been exposed and could still be in third-party logs."

— Tyler Murphy and Ben Weiner, EasyOptOuts

Apple's Fix Under Scrutiny

Questions remain about the completeness of Apple's patch. AppleInsider reported that it successfully reproduced the vulnerability on July 17 — two weeks after Apple's claimed fix date. The publication noted that the test does not prove the flaw remained active for all users or mail providers, but said Apple's assertion of a complete July 3 resolution is difficult to reconcile with independent testing.

Apple has not explained whether the patch was deployed in stages, when the full rollout was completed, or why the July 17 test succeeded. The company has not responded to AppleInsider's request for comment on the discrepancy.

Class Action Lawsuit Filed

The disclosure has also triggered legal action. A proposed class action lawsuit alleges Apple violated California's false advertising law and other consumer protection statutes by marketing Hide My Email as a privacy tool while knowing it did not work as advertised. The plaintiffs seek recovery of subscription fees paid for the feature and an injunction against what the complaint calls Apple's "deceptive conduct."

The lawsuit does not allege that the named plaintiff's address was actually exposed or that anyone exploited the vulnerability maliciously. There is no public evidence of a coordinated exploitation campaign.

What Users Should Do Now

Security researchers say users do not need to disable Hide My Email entirely. However, anyone who created aliases before July 7, 2026 should assume the real addresses behind those aliases may have been disclosed. Deleting an alias will not erase information already retained in another provider's email logs.

The vulnerability did not expose passwords, compromise Apple Accounts, or grant access to inboxes. The demonstrated consequence was limited to revealing the real email address behind a specific alias, which could allow cross-referencing with information from data breaches or public sources.

Apple has not announced any plans to notify affected users or offer remediation beyond the patch itself.
